---
title: "Question 2: Does It Beat a Simple Model?"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/common.R")
fc <- readRDS("data/forecast.rds")
tst <- fc$test
res <- fc$results
full <- res[1, ]
post <- res[2, ]
auc <- fc$auc_eval
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(month = tst$month, series = "Actual incidents", value = tst$actual),
  data.frame(month = tst$month, series = "VendorScore forecast", value = tst$vendorscore),
  data.frame(month = tst$month, series = "12-month average", value = tst$naive))
cum_end <- tail(tst$cum_diff, 1)
cum_shift <- tst$cum_diff[tst$month == 36]
```

## The question

A sophisticated model earns its fee only if it beats a plain alternative. NorthPoint's plain
alternative is a 12-month rolling average of past incident counts. The question: does
VendorScore forecast the bank's monthly incident total better than that average, and does
any advantage survive the deterioration in vendor patching after month 36?

## Method in brief

Each month, VendorScore's portfolio forecast is the sum of its 300 vendor scores. The
benchmark is the average of the previous 12 months' actual incident counts, computed so
that month *t* uses only months before *t*. We compare both with actual incident totals
over months 31 to 48, an out-of-sample, out-of-time window.

We summarise accuracy with mean squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE), and test
equal accuracy with a Diebold–Mariano test using the Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold small-sample
correction, from the `forecastdom` package. We run it twice: over months 31 to 48, and over
months 37 to 48 only, after the shift. Rival approaches, such as encompassing tests or
superior-predictive-ability tests, ask related questions but need longer series.

## Findings

```{r}
#| label: fig-forecast
#| fig-cap: "Monthly incident totals versus both forecasts, months 31–48. The vertical line marks month 36, the last month before patching latency drifts."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of actual monthly incident counts, the VendorScore forecast and the 12-month average, with a vertical line at month 36."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
ggplot(long, aes(month, value, colour = series, linetype = series)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fc$shift_month, colour = "grey50", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = subset(long, series == "Actual incidents"), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Actual incidents" = okabe_ito[["blue"]],
                                 "VendorScore forecast" = okabe_ito[["orange"]],
                                 "12-month average" = okabe_ito[["grey"]])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Actual incidents" = "solid",
                                   "VendorScore forecast" = "solid",
                                   "12-month average" = "longdash")) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Incidents per month (portfolio)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** Blue dots joined by a line are the actual number of incidents
across all 300 vendors each month. The orange line is what VendorScore forecast. The
grey dashed line is the simple 12-month average. The dotted vertical line marks when vendor
patching began to slow.

**What the plot tells you.** Actual incidents trend upward and swing widely from month to
month. The 12-month average trails the trend, forecasting too low for most of the window.
VendorScore sits closer to the level of incidents but is far smoother than the actual
series, so it misses most month-to-month swings. Neither forecast predicts individual
spikes.
:::

Both forecasts are too smooth to follow individual months, but they differ in level. The
12-month average under-forecast by `r num(full$bias_naive, 1)` incidents a month on average, because it
looks backwards while incidents rise. VendorScore's average miss was `r num(full$bias_vs, 1)`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cumulative
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative loss differential, months 31–48. Above zero, VendorScore has accumulated lower squared error than the 12-month average."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the running total of squared-error differences, ending positive, with a vertical line at month 36."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(tst, aes(month, cum_diff)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fc$shift_month, colour = "grey50", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_area(fill = okabe_ito[["blue"]], alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(colour = okabe_ito[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Cumulative squared-error advantage")
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** Each month we ask which forecast was closer to the truth and by
how much. The line keeps a running total: it rises when VendorScore wins a month, falls
when the 12-month average wins, and the height is the net advantage so far.

**What the plot tells you.** The line ends at `r num(cum_end, 1)` above zero, so VendorScore has a net
advantage. It rises only `r num(cum_shift, 1)` by month 36 and `r num(cum_end - cum_shift, 1)` more afterwards, and it
climbs unevenly, with several losing months. A tidy upward line would be stronger evidence;
this one is a mixed record with a favourable tilt.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Forecast accuracy and Diebold–Mariano tests (benchmark versus VendorScore). A positive statistic favours VendorScore."
tab <- data.frame(
  Window = c("Months 31–48 (n = 18)", "Months 37–48 (n = 12)"),
  `MSE 12-month` = res$mse_naive, `MSE VendorScore` = res$mse_vs,
  `MAE 12-month` = res$mae_naive, `MAE VendorScore` = res$mae_vs,
  `DM statistic` = res$dm_stat, `p-value` = res$dm_p, check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, digits = c(0, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3))
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** Each row is a stretch of months. Error columns show the typical
miss in incidents per month for each forecast, so smaller is better. MSE punishes large
misses more heavily than MAE does. The last two columns test whether the gap is real or
could be luck: a small p-value (below 0.05) means luck is an unlikely explanation.

**What the table tells you.** VendorScore has lower errors in both windows, but p-values of
`r pval(full$dm_p)` and `r pval(post$dm_p)` are well above 0.05. Eighteen months, and twelve after the
shift, are too few to separate a modest edge from chance. The result is "no detectable advantage,"
not proof that the two are equal.
:::

VendorScore's MSE is `r pct(1 - full$mse_vs / full$mse_naive, 0)` lower over the full window and
`r pct(1 - post$mse_vs / post$mse_naive, 0)` lower after the shift. The MAE advantage is smaller, and
after the shift almost vanishes (`r num(post$mae_vs, 2)` versus `r num(post$mae_naive, 2)`). A non-significant test with n = 18 has low power,
so it means no detectable advantage, not equality. The pre-shift record is also thin: months
31 to 36 contribute only six observations.

The vendor's AUC of 0.81 is measured on its own development data. It cannot show that
VendorScore stays reliable at *this* bank after conditions change. As a rough check,
NorthPoint's own outcomes give an AUC of `r num(auc["all"], 2)` over months 31 to 48:
`r num(auc["pre"], 2)` for months 31 to 36 and `r num(auc["post"], 2)` afterwards. These come with no interval and few incidents, so
a drop of a few points could be noise. Only ongoing monitoring at the bank can answer the
question (§VII).

## So what

On this evidence, VendorScore gets the level of incidents roughly right and the simple
benchmark does not, but the advantage is statistically unproven and concentrated in a
period when the benchmark lagged a rising trend. The comparison is about aggregate counts,
not about whether individual vendors are ranked correctly.

The April 2026 interagency *Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management* treats
out-of-sample and out-of-time testing and benchmarking as part of model testing (§IV) and
ongoing monitoring (§V). The cumulative-differential chart is the kind of metric that fits
there: it turns "is the model still earning its place?" into a line a committee can watch.
This is partial validation: it tests outputs, not the proprietary method.

## Committee action

Sound practice suggests benchmarking every vendor model against a named simple
alternative, out of sample and out of time, and adding the loss differential to ongoing
monitoring so that deterioration triggers review.
